claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy lacks nanoscale precipitates or ordered domains.
The absence of nanoscale precipitates or ordered domains causes the relatively low hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi.
The initial equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is an as-cast or annealed single-phase solid solution.
The initial alloy has favorable plasticity and machinability.
Aging CoCrFeNiTi at approximately 500–650 °C can induce nanoscale precipitates or an order–disorder transformation.
The aging treatment will form coherent or semi-coherent nanoscale precipitates or ordered domains within the solid solution.
The resulting nanoscale features obstruct dislocation glide.
Obstruction of dislocation glide by the nanoscale features increases hardness and yield strength.
Finely dispersed precipitates can preserve some ductility while increasing strength.
Aged samples will show a statistically significant increase in hardness relative to the untreated alloy.
Aged samples will show a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
An optimal aging treatment can improve strength without complete loss of ductility.
Precipitate coarsening during over-aging may embrittle the alloy.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested from 25 °C to 600 °C under hardness, tensile, or compressive loading.
A loss of ductility following strengthening is indicative of over-aging or embrittlement.

contradictions.description: Embrittlement is presented as a foreseeable consequence of over-aging that controlled processing should avoid, but the falsification rule also treats an undefined 'unacceptable' ductility loss as falsifying the general strengthening hypothesis. Such a result could instead support the proposed over-aging branch while failing only the ductility-retention objective.
